2. Citizen Suits. Laidlaw has spawned not just articles, but whole 
symposia devoted both to that case and to other “citizen suit” litigation. See, 
e.g.. Symposium, Citizen Suits and the Future of Standing in the 21st Century: 
From Lujan to Laidlaw and Beyond, 12 DUKE En v t l . L. & POL’Y F. 1 (2001). 
Combining treatment of Massachusetts v. EPA and Laidlaw, Professor Daniel 
Farber argues for a simplification of environmental standing analysis through 
the application of an easily-stated criterion: a plaintiff has standing to contest 
environmental violations involving a specific area provided the plaintiff can 
show an appropriate relationship to that area. See Daniel A. Farber, A Place- 
Based Theory of Standing, 55 U.C.L.A. L. Re v . 1505 (2008).
3. STATUTORY STANDING AND PUBLIC ACTIONS
At the beginning of our discussion of standing doctrine, we described 
the Sanders Bros, line of cases where challengers proceeded under statutes 
that provided judicial review to any person “adversely affected or 
aggrieved” by agency action. These statutes were sometimes described as 
creating “public actions” in which the plaintiffs served as private attorneys 
general representing the interests of the public. See M. Elizabeth Magill, 
Standing for the Public: A Lost History, 95 Va . L. Re v . 1131 (2009). But as 
noted in that prior discussion, and as has been borne out by subsequent 
standing decisions, that explanation implicitly assumes what the Supreme 
Court has denied—namely, that Congress can provide standing to 
whomever it pleases. Lujan stands for the proposition that the Article III 
requirements can be a powerful barrier to plaintiffs even when Congress 
has clearly sought to enlist so-called “private attorneys general” in the 
enforcement of regulatory statutes.
Nevertheless, Congress has continued to use the “any person 
aggrieved” language in authorizing judicial review, sometimes even 
authorizing “any person” to bring suit (most conspicuously in the citizen 
enforcement provisions that are appended to a number of environmental 
statutes). Moreover, some suits against the federal government are 
brought by public attorneys general representing the interests of their 
states. Does standing doctrine demand the same level of particularized, 
non-speculative and remediable injuries from these parties as from private 
plaintiffs pursuing narrower, private interests?
